fix(project): a rule file's frontmatter is re-derived, not inherited (S16)

A generated rule file's frontmatter was whatever this tool emitted the first time it
saw that surface, and nothing could change it after that. Not `sync`, not `check`, not
`upgrade`.

Two causes, and only the first was the one named. The obvious one was
`extractFrontmatter(existing) ?? frontmatterBlock(mine)`: the file's own block won
whenever the file already had one. But the visible cause was the next line — when the
existing region parsed cleanly, `composed` was the *whole existing file*, so `inject`
replaced the region between the markers and left everything above them untouched.

That is why no gate could have reported it. `check` compares region bodies, and the
body was correct; the frontmatter is not part of the region. The file agreed with
itself, so nothing was stale by any comparison the tool makes, while a surface that
added a key or whose `alwaysApply` flipped could never reach a repository that had
already adopted it.

The fix swaps the block in place rather than stripping it and rejoining, and the reason
is a mistake worth recording. My first version rebuilt the file as
`frontmatter + "\n" + bodyAfterFrontmatter(existing)`; that helper's trailing `\n*`
swallows the blank line a formatter requires before an HTML comment, so the
reconstruction was one newline short of the file. `inject` compares the spliced result
against what it was given, so it reported `updated` on every run, forever, while
writing identical bytes — 1948 -> 1948, and again, and again. The file was right; the
verdict never settled, so `check` reported drift no reader could see and `sync` rewrote
a correct file on every invocation. Rebuilding a file has to reproduce the bytes it did
not mean to touch, and the cheapest way to guarantee that is not to rebuild them.

One asymmetry, stated as a test because it is the only place this deletes something: a
surface that emits no frontmatter leaves an existing block alone. This tool owns the
block it writes and will replace it; removing a block it did not write is a different
operation.

Four tests, two mutations: reverting to inheritance fails on its own assertion, and the
strip-and-rejoin I actually shipped is caught by the convergence tests. Zero churn
across the estate — 14 repositories, no target changes — so nothing to roll out.
777/777.
